claims.text: The damaged nickel-based superalloy surface has coarse grains and microsegregated regions.
Previous fusion-welding repairs make the component prone to hot cracking.
A rotating-tool FSP intervention can be applied to the damaged nickel-based superalloy surface.
Suitable FSP rotation rates are 400–600 rpm.
The specified FSP conditions will produce a stirred layer less than 1 mm deep.
The FSP treatment occurs below the alloy's melting temperature.
Ambient-atmosphere processing with controlled cooling will prevent overheating.
Real-time temperature and load monitoring combined with post-process mapping will ensure treatment uniformity.
FSP will refine the near-surface grain structure.
FSP will eliminate or homogenize near-surface microsegregation.
The rotating tool induces severe plastic deformation that causes grain refinement and chemical homogenization.
Grain refinement and chemical homogenization lower local stress concentrations.
Lower local stress concentrations suppress hot-crack initiation and propagation during thermal and mechanical service.
The modified near-surface region will form a metastable layer resistant to crack initiation and propagation.
FSP will produce higher surface hardness than both an untreated damaged surface and a traditional fusion-weld repair.
FSP will improve wear resistance relative to both an untreated damaged surface and a traditional fusion-weld repair.
FSP will reduce hot-cracking tendency relative to both an untreated damaged surface and a traditional fusion-weld repair.
The predicted benefits will persist at elevated temperatures and in aggressive wear environments.
The treatment may be ineffective when defects extend deeper than the shallow stirred layer or service temperatures exceed the layer's thermal stability.
